title: Legume cover crops / legume rotation
action: Add a legume cover crop or rotation phase (cowpea, vetch, clover, lentil) between main crops.
why: Legume roots and residues feed soil microbes and fix nitrogen, cutting fertiliser need, while extra biomass builds soil organic carbon. In water-limited sites use short-season legumes and terminate them early so they do not drain soil moisture.
effect: Cover crops add ~0.3 Mg C/ha/yr on average (global meta-analysis); slow but compounding.
source: Poeplau & Don (2015), Agric. Ecosyst. Environ. 200:33-41; FAO (2017) Soil Organic Carbon: the hidden potential

title: Agroforestry (trees integrated with crops)
action: Integrate multipurpose native/nitrogen-fixing trees in alleys or field boundaries (e.g., 5-10% of land), using species suited to local rainfall.
why: Trees add litter and deep roots (raising soil carbon and infiltration), provide shade that lowers soil temperature and evaporation, and create habitat and stepping-stones that reconnect fragmented landscapes.
effect: European meta-analysis found higher biodiversity and better soil fertility / erosion control than treeless farming; IPCC lists agroforestry as an adaptation + mitigation option with soil-carbon co-benefits.
source: Torralba et al. (2016), Agric. Ecosyst. Environ. 230:150-161; IPCC SRCCL (2019) Ch. 6

title: Intercropping and multi-crop rotations
action: Replace single-crop cycles with intercropping (cereal + legume) or a 3+ crop rotation including a deep-rooted crop.
why: Diverse root systems and residues support broader microbial and invertebrate communities, break pest cycles (reducing pesticide need), and spread water and nutrient use across soil layers.
effect: Crop diversification raised on-farm biodiversity by ~24% on average in a global meta-analysis; yield effects are variable, so pilot on part of the land first.
source: Beillouin et al. (2021), Global Change Biology 27:4697-4710; Tamburini et al. (2020), Science Advances 6:eaba1715

title: Reduced tillage with residue mulching
action: Move to no-till / minimum tillage and keep crop residue as surface mulch.
why: Mulch cuts evaporation and buffers soil temperature, protecting soil fauna; undisturbed aggregates hold water better. Note: carbon gains are mostly near the surface and smaller than often claimed, so the main win is moisture and soil-life protection.
effect: No-till with residue retention and rotation performs comparably or better than conventional tillage in dry climates.
source: Pittelkow et al. (2015), Nature 517:365-368; Powlson et al. (2014), Nature Climate Change 4:678-683

title: Rainwater harvesting (contour bunds, swales, farm ponds)
action: Build contour bunds / swales and small farm ponds to slow runoff and recharge soil and groundwater.
why: In low-rainfall areas most water is lost as runoff. Capturing it extends soil moisture into dry spells, sustains vegetation and wetlands species, and supports tree establishment.
effect: Improves infiltration and growing-season moisture; magnitude is site-specific, so measure with soil-moisture sensors or NDMI before/after.
horizon: Short (<1 year to build; benefits within 1-2 seasons)
source: IPCC AR6 WGII (2022) Ch. 5; FAO water-harvesting guidance

title: Lime application to correct soil acidity
action: Apply agricultural lime based on a soil buffer-pH test, targeting pH ~6-7, ideally combined with organic matter.
why: Soil pH is the strongest predictor of soil bacterial diversity; acidity also suppresses decomposition and legume nodulation, so lime should come before legume-based interventions.
effect: Bacterial diversity peaks near neutral pH; correcting acidity restores microbial function within 1-2 seasons.

title: Compost / manure / biochar amendments
action: Apply compost or well-rotted manure (and optionally biochar) each season, targeted to the poorest zones.
why: Organic amendments directly add carbon and nutrients, stimulate microbial biomass, improve aggregate structure and water retention, and buffer high pH.
effect: Long-term studies show consistent increases in soil organic carbon and microbial activity with organic amendments.

title: Hedgerows and flower strips on field margins
action: Plant native flowering hedgerows or 3-6 m wildflower strips along field edges and drainage lines.
why: They provide nesting and forage for pollinators and natural enemies of pests, act as corridors between habitat patches, and trap spray drift and runoff.
effect: Synthesis of field studies shows flower strips and hedgerows improve pollination and pest control services.
source: Albrecht et al. (2020), Ecology Letters 23:1488-1498; Kremen & Miles (2012), Ecology and Society 17(4):40

title: Habitat corridors linking remnant patches
action: Restore vegetated corridors (or stepping-stone patches) between remaining natural habitat fragments.
why: Fragmentation isolates populations and reduces biodiversity; corridors restore movement, gene flow and recolonisation.
effect: Fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13-75% across studies; corridors raise movement between patches by ~50% on average.
source: Haddad et al. (2015), Science Advances 1:e1500052; Gilbert-Norton et al. (2010), Conservation Biology 24:660-668

title: Integrated pest management (IPM) and input reduction
action: Adopt IPM: scouting thresholds, biological control, targeted (not calendar) spraying, and buffer strips near habitats.
why: Pesticide use has persistent negative effects on farmland biodiversity and natural pest control; lowering exposure lets predators and pollinators recover.
effect: Reduced pesticide intensity is associated with higher farmland biodiversity and biological control potential.
source: Geiger et al. (2010), Basic and Applied Ecology 11:97-105

title: Vegetated riparian / drainage buffer strips
action: Establish perennial native vegetation strips along streams, ditches and ponds.
why: Buffers filter sediment and nutrients before they reach water bodies, stabilise banks, and keep aquatic and amphibian habitat viable.
effect: Reviews report substantial reductions in sediment and nutrient loads; efficacy depends on buffer width and slope.
source: Zhang et al. (2010), J. Environ. Quality 39:76-84

title: Assisted natural regeneration
action: Protect cleared or degraded plots from grazing and fire, remove invasives, and let native vegetation regrow, supplementing with targeted planting.
why: Where seed sources and soil seedbanks remain, natural regeneration recovers biodiversity better and cheaper than full planting.
effect: Natural regeneration outperformed active restoration for biodiversity and structure recovery in tropical forests.

title: Drought/heat-tolerant native and locally adapted species mixes
action: Shift to drought-tolerant crops (millets, sorghum + legume mixes) and native shade/forage trees suited to projected climate.
why: Rising temperature and erratic rainfall push non-adapted species past physiological limits; adapted mixes maintain ground cover, soil carbon and habitat through dry spells.
effect: Climate-adapted diversification is a recognised adaptation option; benefits are strongest when combined with mulching or water harvesting.
source: IPCC AR6 WGII (2022) Ch. 5; FAO climate-smart agriculture guidance
